summary: Find what tgrep does differently in its one-shot search path and which techniques loomux graph grep can adopt

result.gap:
The tgrep figures are from the runtime run: 19.5 ms literal, 56.6 ms alternation, 86.2 ms -i (one-shot). The loomux figures are the per-phase medians of S1-S12 on a clean tree (literal 87.5 ms, alternation 119.3 ms). Each line below reads loomux vs tgrep.

LITERAL (gap about 68 ms):
- Process start: 15 vs 9.5 ms (+5.5). loomux loads a 40.7 MB image and runs 163 package inits, 4.6 ms of them for tree-sitter grammars, net, wiki, benchsearch and verify/commit.
- Freshness probe: 42.2 vs 0 ms (+42). This is the walk (27-35) plus a decode of fingerprint.json.gob and a compare against the graph (about 7-10). tgrep's one-shot does no walk and no stat; it trusts the index blindly. That is the main gap, and most of it is the price of correctness.
- State decode and recompute: spans 4.2 + corpus record 3.1 + rules 4.1 + listing derive and second drift compare 6.2 + 0.5, about 18 vs 0 ms (+18). tgrep has no symbol enrichment, no second drift record, and its ignore state is precomputed in files-extra.bin. loomux re-parses ignore bodies, rebuilds trackedDirs over about 8400 paths, and runs SearchCorpus twice, on every call.
- Index open and lookup: 7.3 vs about 8 ms (even). tgrep also does wasteful work here (blake3 of files.bin, a sort of 8.4k paths, meta.json parsed twice).
- Verification: 1.8 vs about 2 ms (even). loomux has 73 candidates read in parallel; tgrep has 9-10 read serially at about 0.24 ms each.
- Output and exit: 4-5 vs <1 ms (+4). loomux builds the whole result with MarshalIndent into one buffer; tgrep streams through an 8 KiB BufWriter.

ALTERNATION 'Search|Grep' (gap about 63 ms):
- The fixed part is the same as for the literal, about 85 ms vs 17.5 ms.
- Verification is about even: loomux 31 ms in parallel over 488 files, tgrep about 39 ms serial over 109 files at 0.36 ms each.
- loomux reads 4x more files because its index is lowercase-only (trigram.go:5-51 folds every window). LITPRE also lowercases the literals and makes an asciiLower copy of every candidate.
- Checked with git grep: case-exact `Search|Grep` matches 120 files, case-folded matches 354. tgrep's 120 raw candidates equal the exact count. This is also the most likely cause of the unexplained 31 ms vs the 9-12 ms in the doc.

-i: parity (tgrep 86-120 ms vs loomux 80-136 ms). tgrep pays about 0.37 ms per file serially over 188 candidates, which offsets loomux's fixed overhead. loomux's index is already case-folded, so the source investigation's claim that loomux lacks folded trigrams is wrong. What loomux lacks is the case-EXACT trigrams.

NO LITERAL: loomux wins by about 20x (230-330 ms vs 5200-6700 ms). tgrep's indexed path verifies serially and opens each file with per-path-component handles plus three GetFinalPathNameByHandleW calls; -j has no effect.

CRLF is not a factor in this repo: .gitattributes sets `* text=auto eol=lf`, and none of the 354 folded candidates contains \r. The S5/S12 \r fallback only matters in CRLF repos.

FLOOR: a Windows one-shot that stays correct cannot go below the walk (about 27-35 ms) plus process start (about 10-15 ms), so about 45 ms. Candidates C3-C8 below, without a daemon or journal, should bring the literal from about 87 to about 55-60 ms and the alternation from about 119 to about 70-80 ms. tgrep's 20-60 ms is reachable only without the walk, which needs C1 (daemon with cookie fence) or C2 (USN journal). Several of these are already being spiked in another session (untracked zz_spike_mmap*.go, zz_spike_spanidx.go, zz_spike_trust.go).
not_transferable: tgrep one-shot 'trust the index' (no walk, no stat, filestamps never read) and its loomux copy, spike TRUST (zz_spike_trust.go: listing taken from the record or index under --no-refresh). Measured: a new file is invisible even when -g names it, and an edit that adds the pattern to a file whose old content lacked the trigrams is missed. That violates the hard requirement. Only acceptable behind C1's fence or C2's journal.

tgrep server as it ships (eventually consistent, no barrier, edit visible after about 40-65 ms, the first query after a write misses). Transferable only with the cookie fence and overflow rescan in C1.

Directory mtimes as a cheaper freshness check. On NTFS and ext4 a directory's LastWriteTime changes only when an entry in that directory is created, deleted or renamed. In-place content edits and changes in grandchildren do not bump it, so every file still needs its own stat. On Windows os.ReadDir already returns size and mtime in bulk (FindNextFile / FileIdBothDirectoryInfo), so skipping ReadDir for unchanged dirs and stat-ing 8400 files one by one would be SLOWER. On Linux it would save only the getdents calls, not the 8400 lstats. Net saving is about 0, and the risk of a stale directory index is real.

git index stat data (.git/index ctime, mtime, size per tracked file). It covers tracked files only, so untracked files still need a walk; the per-file comparison is no cheaper than the bulk ReadDir walk loomux already does; and racy-git entries need content checks anyway. git's untracked cache adds the directory-mtime problem above. Optional variant: when the user has core.fsmonitor (git's builtin fsmonitor daemon) enabled, asking it for changes since a token over its pipe is a correct cheaper check. It is opt-in and absent by default, so it is at most a fast path in front of the walk, not a replacement.

Folding ASCII-lowercase trigrams for -i (source investigation COPY 1). loomux already has this: trigram.go folds every window, and -i is at parity or faster than tgrep. The missing half is case-exact trigrams (C3).

Serial candidate verification and the 'rooted' per-component open (verify_root, CreateFile, three GetFinalPathNameByHandleW calls per component). This is 0.24-0.87 ms per file and why tgrep takes 5.2-6.7 s for no-literal regexes. loomux's 16 parallel readers with plain os.ReadFile are already about 20x faster there.
mmap of candidate files: tgrep itself does it only for files of 1 MiB and up. The Go os.ReadFile with a stat-sized buffer already matches tgrep COPY 3, and fusing the NUL check would save <1 ms here.

tgrep's index-open waste: blake3 of the whole files.bin, a sort of all 8427 paths, meta.json parsed twice, 2.7 MB JSON filestamps, all match rows as one JSON line over TCP, serial cache-miss reads in the server, and an unused loc_mask. None of these should be copied.
Custom allocator: tgrep uses the system allocator, so there is nothing to copy. GC off (S10) was already measured as noise.

S12/S5 \r fallback improvements (tgrep strips \r per line after a whole-buffer pass): transferable in principle but worth nothing in this repo. .gitattributes sets `* text=auto eol=lf`, and none of the 354 folded candidates contains \r. Relevant only for CRLF repos.

candidates.title: Resident daemon: recursive watcher plus a cookie-file fence, so warm queries skip the walk
candidates.tgrep_does: `tgrep serve` keeps the mmapped index, an in-memory overlay of changed files (hybrid.rs:120-282), an LRU of decoded file text (50k entries / 1 GiB) and a recursive ReadDirectoryChangesW watcher. Warm queries take 0.2-3 ms in the server and about 17-25 ms at the client. It has NO read-your-writes barrier: handle_search takes no snapshot_gate (serve.rs:1963-2001), and an edit shows up only after about 40-65 ms. The first query after a write was measured missing.
candidates.loomux_does: One-shot. Every call walks the tree (27-35 ms), compares two drift records and decodes about 20 MB of state.
candidates.change:
Add an opt-in `loomux grep-daemon` per root.
- On start: one full walk plus a stamp compare, the same as today; answer nothing until that is done.
- Then keep in memory the stamp table, the trigram index, spans, rules, and an overlay of changed or new paths (scanned in full, as S4 does).
- Watcher: on Windows a single ReadDirectoryChangesW handle with bWatchSubtree=TRUE via x/sys/windows (fsnotify is per-directory, so not that); on Linux inotify per directory.
- Fence before every answer, Watchman-style: create `.loomux/state/cookie-<nonce>` in the root and block until the watcher reports it. A single recursive handle delivers events in order, so every write before the query has then been seen.
- On ERROR_NOTIFY_ENUM_DIR or an inotify queue overflow, do a full rescan before answering.
- If an ignore file changes, rebuild the rules.
- The client falls back to the one-shot when no daemon answers within a few ms.
- Transport: a named pipe or Unix socket with an ACL limited to the current user, not TCP.
- Files: new internal/code/daemon/{server,watch_windows,watch_linux,fence}.go, the client switch in internal/cli/graph.go, and a reuse of query.Grep with injected state.
candidates.saving_ms_windows: About 50-60 on literal (87 -> about 25-35: 13 client start + IPC + fence + in-memory query; the doc measured 25 ms in-process without a walk). About 50-60 on alternation.
candidates.saving_ms_linux: About 25-30 (42 -> about 10-15; client start about 5 ms).
candidates.risk: High complexity: daemon lifecycle (start, crash, stale pid, several roots, binary upgrade), a secured local channel, watcher edge cases (network drives, WSL paths, overflow), and memory use. The cookie fence costs 1-3 ms and needs write access to the root. This contradicts the current one-shot design, so it is a separate decision (flagged in the doc's Empfehlung).

verdict.corrected_saving_ms: Windows: about 50-65 ms on literal (86-98 with the check, down to about 20-30; the floor matches the S13-S16 trust mode at 23 ms one-shot, and the in-memory query is about 5 ms). About 60-70 ms on alternation (102-107 down to about 35-40). Linux: about 25-30 ms (42 down to about 10-15). The 1-3 ms fence cost is not measured yet.
verdict.correctness_issue: The proposal is correct on a modified tree only if its ignore handling is extended. In C:\Users\micro\Documents\#GIT\loomux\.claude\worktrees\spike-grep-startup\internal\code\corpus\ignore.go:100-120 and 349-365, the rules depend on things outside the watched root. These are .git/index (the tracked set, which changes on `git add -f` and `git rm --cached`; a tracked file is never ignored), .git/config (core.ignorecase and core.excludesFile), the info/exclude file and the global excludes file. In a linked worktree (exactly this setup, under .claude/worktrees), gitPath resolves all of these into the main repo's .git directory, outside the root. A recursive watcher on the root never sees them change. "Rebuild rules if an ignore file changes" therefore misses them, and the daemon would silently return or drop files wrongly. Fix: before each answer, stat the IndexStamp, ConfigStamp and GitPaths stamps the record already keeps (well under 1 ms), and rebuild the rules on any change. Other gaps to handle: (1) ReadDirectoryChangesW reports a directory rename (or moving a directory in from outside) only as the directory itself, so the daemon must rescan that subtree; on Linux the same applies to directories created before their inotify watch is added. (2) .loomux/state rewritten by another process (graph build) must invalidate the in-memory index, spans and records. (3) Network drives, SUBST and \\wsl$ roots, plus read-only roots where the cookie cannot be written, must fall back to the one-shot. (4) NTFS reports writes lazily on handles that stay open. This is not a regression, because the current walk reads FindNextFile metadata (walk.go:165 d.Info()), which is updated just as lazily. CRLF and case-insensitive non-ASCII folds are not affected, provided query.Grep is reused unchanged (S11 skips non-ASCII files under -i, S12 sends files with \r line by line). Deleted and new files are covered by watcher events plus the S4 overlay, and by a full rescan on overflow.
verdict.reasoning:
Checked the tgrep claims against its source (tgrep-cli/src/serve.rs). handle_search (line 1963) takes only state.index.read() and visibility, with no snapshot_gate, cookie or barrier anywhere. The watcher batches events with WATCHER_BURST_QUIET 25 ms and WATCHER_BURST_MAX 100 ms (lines 95-96), which fits edits becoming visible after about 40-65 ms. On Windows it uses notify with RecursiveMode::Recursive, a single recursive ReadDirectoryChangesW handle (lines 3184-3190). The decoded-file LRU (lines 314-380) and the live overlay in hybrid.rs exist. So the claimed tgrep behaviour holds: fast but no read-your-writes.

Saving against the phase bound: the doc's phase trace after S7-S10 on Windows (literal) is walk plus record compare 32-34, spans 4.6, record 3-4, rules 7-10, index 6-8 and search 2 ms. On top come about 13 ms process start and about 20 ms not attributed, for 86-98 ms end to end. A daemon removes every phase except search, client start, IPC and fence, so the removable part is about 55-60 ms in process plus part of the unattributed time. A 50-60 ms saving does not exceed it. Independent check: the S13-S16 trust mode, which skips the walk and records and mmaps the index, measures 23 ms one-shot. A daemon with in-memory state plus a fence should land at about 20-30 ms, which confirms the 25-35 target and the saving. Linux: total 39-43 ms, of which process start is 5 ms and loadGraph plus state decoding about 27-35 ms, so 25-30 ms saved is within bound.

Correctness: the cookie fence over a single recursive handle (or a single inotify fd) is ordered, so it gives read-your-writes for writes inside the root, which tgrep lacks. That makes it sound in principle. However, the ignore rules (ignore.go) depend on .git/index, .git/config, info/exclude and global excludes, which lie outside the root in a linked worktree. That needs per-query stamp checks the proposal does not list. Directory renames need subtree rescans. These are fixable and cost under 1 ms, so the candidate holds with those amendments. It does not hold as literally specified ("rebuild rules if an ignore file changes"). Not measured by me: fence latency and actual daemon IPC time, and the saving rests on the doc's in-process and trust-mode figures.

candidates.title: Windows: replace the walk with an NTFS USN journal read plus the stored stamp table
candidates.tgrep_does: Nothing comparable. The one-shot skips freshness entirely, and the server walks the tree for 103 ms at start, then relies on the watcher.
candidates.loomux_does: A full parallel walk of about 3300 dirs and 8400 entries on every call, 27-35 ms, saturated at 16 readers.
candidates.saving_ms_windows: About 25-30 when it works (walk 27-35 -> about 2-5 for the journal read and a few stats). 0 when it falls back.
candidates.risk:
High and UNVERIFIED:
- Reading \\.\C: normally needs admin. Whether FSCTL_READ_UNPRIVILEGED_USN_JOURNAL works for a normal user on this Windows build, and returns enough (names, parent FRN), must be spiked first. If it does not, the candidate is dead.
- Journal records are volume-wide: a busy volume (browser caches, builds) can mean thousands of records to skip.
- No journal on FAT, network shares or some VM mounts.
- Hard links and renames across the root boundary need care.
Windows-only code path.

verdict.corrected_saving_ms: 0 in practice, and often negative. The most it could ever save is the walk inside loadGraph (about 27 ms of the 32-34 ms phase). Reading the whole journal unprivileged took 25-100 ms warm and 357 ms cold (420k records, 39 MB), which is as slow as the walk or slower. Each one-shot call has to re-read everything written since the stored USN, so the cost grows with volume activity until the next build. On top of that, the journal returns no file names, so every relevant record costs an extra by-ID name lookup.
verdict.correctness_issue: The unprivileged journal read returns no names: 0 of about 420k records had a FileName. So the plan as written (match by parent FRN, then turn records into paths) cannot see new or renamed files without an extra OpenFileById plus a name query per record, and that path is unverified. Changed files need an FRN map of all ~8400 files, not only the ~3300 directories. A .gitignore change can let in files under directories that were ignored, and those directories are not in the map, so any .gitignore change must fall back to the full walk. The journal wraps within minutes under build load (about 4.5 MB in 30 s), which makes the fallback the common case. A hard link or a change made through another path changes the file without a record under the parent FRN we watch. CRLF files and -i non-ASCII folds are not affected, because the search stays the same.
verdict.reasoning:
tgrep claim: true. The tgrep source has no USN or journal code at all, only filestamps.json.

Measured on this machine without admin rights (probe in C:\Users\micro\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\5f6807b516805710\fcefffaa-a51a-403b-8401-af2bb7918cb7\scratchpad\usnprobe\main.go):
(1) Opening \\.\C: for reading: access denied. With access 0 the query fails with 'invalid function'. FSCTL_READ_USN_JOURNAL fails with access denied on every handle.
(2) FSCTL_READ_UNPRIVILEGED_USN_JOURNAL works through a directory handle with READ_USN_JOURNAL_DATA_V1, but FileNameLength is 0 on all 420k records. Records carry only FRN, parent FRN and reason.
(3) Reading the full journal (39 MB, about 420k records) took 357 ms cold and 25-100 ms warm. Reading from a USN that is not on a record boundary returns ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER.
(4) NextUsn grew by about 4.5 MB in 30 s while builds were running. Against a 32 MB maximum, the journal wraps within minutes. Each read-only one-shot call must scan everything since the stored USN, so in the common case the cost reaches or passes the full-journal cost, or the call falls back to the walk.

Ceiling: the research doc puts the walk at about 27 ms. It is the bulk of the loadGraph phase (32-34 ms), so the claimed 25-30 ms is the absolute maximum, before counting the journal scan, the per-record name lookups and loading an FRN map of about 8400 files (the doc measures 3-4 ms just to decode the corpus record). The candidate is not dead (unprivileged access works), but as specified it does not work: it assumes names it does not get. The realistic saving is at or below zero, so it fails.

candidates.title: Case-exact trigrams in the index plus a case-exact literal prefilter
candidates.tgrep_does: For every window it inserts BOTH the original trigram and its ASCII-lowercased form into one posting map (trigram.rs:202-283). Case-sensitive queries look up exact keys; -i queries look up the lowercase keys. Result: `Search|Grep` gives 120 raw candidates, `func Search` gives 10.
candidates.loomux_does: The index is lowercase-only (trigram.go:5-51). LITPRE lowercases the literals and makes an asciiLower copy of every candidate. Result: 488 candidates for `Search|Grep`, 73 for `func Search`. git grep confirms 120 files match case-exactly vs 354 case-folded.
candidates.change:
trigram.go: pack the original bytes as the key and additionally insert the folded key when it differs. That is 24-bit keys over raw bytes, the same as tgrep; the lowercase key then serves as the union of all case variants.
literals.go: when the pattern has no FoldCase flag, emit exact literals and do not ToLower them.
grep/zz_spike_scan.go LITPRE:
- case-sensitive patterns: bytes.Contains on the original data, with no asciiLower copy;
- -i patterns: unchanged.
Raise the index format version so an old index triggers a rebuild.
Optional: tgrep's 1-byte next_mask Bloom of the following byte, which removed about 8% of candidates there. Only worth adding if the index format is touched anyway.
candidates.saving_ms_windows: About 15-25 on alternation (search phase 31 -> about 8-12, 4x fewer files read). About 1 on literal. 0 on -i and no-literal.
candidates.risk: Low to medium. The index grows by perhaps 40-80% in postings, and graph build gets slightly slower. Under the current whole-file ReadFile of trigram.idx that costs about +2-4 ms per call, so combine it with C5 (lazy open). Correctness holds: an exact literal is a necessary condition, the folded key stays a superset, and non-ASCII handling is unchanged.

verdict.corrected_saving_ms: Windows alternation: about 3-7 ms net, capped at the 9-12 ms search phase that S11 leaves. A larger trigram.idx makes the trigram phase slower and takes back part of that. Literal: about 0-1 ms. -i and no-literal: 0. Linux: a few ms at most.
verdict.correctness_issue: The LITPRE change as written is unsafe. It picks case-exact bytes.Contains when the CLI -i flag is off, but trigram.Literals also lowercases literals under inline fold flags: a pattern like (?i)search or Foo(?i:bar) without -i. spikeLitSets passes only [][]string plus the CLI ignoreCase, so the per-literal fold information is lost. An exact Contains of the lowercased "search" on the original data rejects a file that contains only "Search", and that hit is silently lost. This is not limited to dirty trees. The fix is to carry a per-literal FoldCase bit, or use the exact path only when no literal came from a FoldCase node. The index side is safe: the folded key stays a superset. CRLF, non-ASCII (still rejected by Pack and literalOf), deleted or new files (the overlay always reads them) and .gitignore changes (rules come from the walk) are not affected.
verdict.reasoning: The tgrep claim is confirmed. tgrep-core/src/trigram.rs:202-283 inserts both the original hash and the ASCII-lowercased hash per window, plus next_mask. query.rs:42-65 sets case_insensitive only for -i, and case-sensitive literal plans use the exact bytes. The loomux claim is confirmed in part. trigram.go Pack and Grams fold to lowercase. literals.go literalOf already keeps case-sensitive literals exact and lowercases only under FoldCase, so that part of the proposed change already exists. zz_spike_scan.go LITPRE lowercases every literal (strings.ToLower) and makes an asciiLower copy of each candidate. The match counts check out: git grep gives 120 files for Search|Grep case-exact against 354 case-folded, and 10 against 13 for func Search. The saving is overstated. The research doc (S11 row) says LITPRE already brought the alternation search phase from 46-57 ms down to 9-12 ms, and S1-S12 includes S11. The "search phase 31 -> 8-12" baseline appears nowhere in the doc. A cut of 15-25 ms cannot come out of a 9-12 ms phase. Reading about 120-130 candidates instead of 488 with 16 parallel readers, and dropping the lowercase copy, plausibly saves 3-7 ms. The larger index (+40-80% postings, read whole without C5) adds back 2-4 ms. My own trace run with all switches gave 225-640 ms search phases and 110-430 ms walks, which points to a loaded machine and possibly a stale graph, so it is unusable. I fell back on the documented phase numbers. One correctness gap: the exact LITPRE path keys on the CLI -i flag and ignores inline (?i), so it can drop real hits.

candidates.title: One stamp table, one compare, with derived ignore state persisted
candidates.tgrep_does: It keeps a single per-path stamp table (filestamps: mtime, size, ns timestamps, content id). The stale check diffs one walk against that one table, and the same walk feeds the ignore matcher (serve.rs:6335-6395, 6940-6980). Visibility and ignore results are precomputed into files-extra.bin at build time, and nothing is evaluated against .gitignore at query time.
candidates.loomux_does:
Two drift records over the same walk:
- fingerprint.json.gob, compared by freshness.Probe, whose result is used only to skip EnsureFresh;
- corpus.json.gob Files, compared by corpus.Compare.
It runs SearchCorpus twice, and a changed file can be sha256-hashed twice. rulesFromRecord rebuilds trackedDirs via path.Dir over about 8400 paths and re-parses every ignore body on every call.
candidates.saving_ms_windows: About 8-12 (rules 4.1 -> <1; derive/compare 6.2 plus probe remainder 5-10 -> one compare of about 3-5; one gob decode instead of two).
candidates.risk: Medium: it touches the graph's and the corpus's freshness contracts at once. The persisted rules must be invalidated by stat of every ignore source, global excludes and core.excludesFile included, or ignore edits are missed. Check equality with DeepEqual against today's two compares on clean and modified trees.

verdict.corrected_saving_ms: Windows about 4-7 ms, which is inside the measured run-to-run noise of 40-80 %; Linux about 3-5 ms. The 8-12 ms (Windows) and 5-8 ms (Linux) estimates are too high.
verdict.correctness_issue: No result-level correctness defect if it is built as described. CRLF, case-insensitive non-ASCII folds and the regex path are untouched, because C4 changes only freshness and corpus selection. New, deleted and changed files come from one compare over the same walk. Ignore edits are already detected by changedSources (stat plus sha256 of each source, and existence of the exclude and global paths), by addedIgnoreFiles, and by the .git/index and .git/config stamps. Persisted rules keyed on those stamps keep that contract, as long as the derive runs only after the source check or its result is thrown away on source drift. There are two real risks. (1) The graph set (sourceset, no matcher, bound to the extractor version) and the corpus set (matcher, binary rule, bound to MaxFilesize and settings) have different membership and different invalidation keys. A merged table must keep both bindings, or a change of extractor or settings would leave the other side marked fresh by mistake. (2) The rule about the tgrep source is partly wrong. tgrep's FileStamp is only {mtime,size}; content ids and versions sit in a separate FileEvidence. files-extra.bin persists visibility only for paths listed by --files, not ignore results. The stale check in tgrep (serve.rs ~6940-6980) builds its ignore matcher live during the walk (walk_file_metadata_with_ignorecase, build_stale_matcher) and runs only in server mode. So tgrep does not show the "persist parsed ignore state" part; that part is new loomux design, not something taken from tgrep.
verdict.reasoning:
Checked the code in the spike worktree. On both a clean tree and a tree with up to 200 changed files, OVERLAY runs freshness.Probe once and then skips EnsureFresh, so there is exactly one probe. Probe decodes fingerprint.json.gob and diffs it against sourceset.Stat. grep.go then reads corpus.json(.gob), calls RulesFromRecord, derives the listing from the memoized walk (deriveListing applies Ignored and Tracked to about 8400 entries), and calls corpus.Compare. Compare calls SearchCorpus internally, and grep.go:188 calls it a second time. So the claims about two records, two compares, SearchCorpus twice and possible double hashing are true.

Measurement: a read-only trace (LMX_SPIKE_TRACE, S1-S12 switches) on a timestamp-preserving robocopy of the tree in the scratchpad, 10 runs, Literal pattern. readRecord 3-4 ms, rules 3.7-5.7 ms (median ~4.3), walk+compare 5.7-9.6 ms (median ~7.5), searchcorpus+channel 0-1.5 ms. loadGraph was not usable in the temp directory (65-300 ms). The research doc gives 32-34 ms for loadGraph, about 27 of it the walk, so roughly 5-7 ms of probe remainder.

Why the claimed saving is too large:
- walk+compare is mostly deriveListing (the matcher over every entry; round 1 measured it at 7.7 ms). C4 still has to do that work to know the corpus membership, so merging the compares saves only the compare part, about 1-3 ms.
- Rules at 4 ms are mostly building the tracked map (~8400 entries) and trackedDirs (~3300). Persisting them as gob maps still means decoding maps, about 1-2 ms rather than under 1 ms. Saving: about 2-3 ms.
- Fingerprint decode plus probe compare: about 2-3 ms saved. The merged table is larger than either record, so only one decode goes away, not all of its cost.
- The second SearchCorpus call is a cheap loop, under 0.5 ms.
- Double hashing applies only to suspect files, about 20 small files in the benchmark, under 1 ms.

Total: about 4-7 ms on Windows and about 3-5 ms on Linux (Linux phases: rules 3-4, compare 3-5). That is below the 8-12 ms claimed for Windows, and the doc reports 40-80 % scatter there, so the gain would not be measurable. The change still has medium risk, because it touches two freshness contracts at once.

candidates.title: Lazy index open: ReadAt/mmap of trigram.idx, an offset-indexed file table, and a stored digest
candidates.tgrep_does: It mmaps lookup.bin and index.bin lazily, with no prefetch, and binary-searches the fixed 16-byte lookup table in place. Only the touched posting pages fault in (reader.rs:192-290, 675-790). The index opens in about 8 ms for 22 MB (tgrep wastes part of that on blake3 and a path sort, which should not be copied).
candidates.loomux_does: os.ReadFile of the whole 13.3 MB trigram.idx even under LAZYIDX. It decodes all of about 7700 file-table strings and recomputes corpus.Digest (copy, sort and sha256 over about 7700 lines) on every call. The 'trigram' phase takes 7.3 ms.
candidates.risk: Low to medium. On Windows a mapped file cannot be replaced while it is mapped, so graph build must write and rename a new file with a retry, or use versioned filenames. ReadAt avoids that and is the simpler first rung. The stored digest must be written atomically with the index it binds.

verdict.corrected_saving_ms: Windows: about 5-9 ms in total, measured in-process. result.src_notes:
I read source tag v1.2.3 (commit 58629d2), cloned to C:\Users\micro\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\5f6807b516805710\fcefffaa-a51a-403b-8401-af2bb7918cb7\scratchpad\tgrep-src. I did not build or run anything from the clone. The only thing I ran was the installed winget tgrep.exe with --stats, from the worktree.

**Why tgrep's one-shot is fast, and where it is slow**
- It is fast only on literals with few candidates (88-109 files). It does no tree walk and no stat of the corpus.
- It loads cheaply: lazy mmap of lookup.bin and index.bin. Even so, it reads all of files.bin, blake3-hashes it, decodes 8.4k Strings and sorts them, and parses meta.json twice.
- Verifying candidates is slow:
  - The loop is serial (search.rs:1788).
  - Each file goes through an expensive "rooted" open on Windows. verify_root runs every time, then for each path component a CreateFile, a metadata call and three GetFinalPathNameByHandleW calls (rooted.rs:204-280).
  - This is about 0.4-0.75 ms per file. It explains the 5.2-5.9 s for MatchAll (7662 files) and the 145 ms for -i (281 files).
- The no-literal case is pure serial I/O. Loomux's 16 parallel readers already beat it by 20x, so there is nothing to copy there.
- Loomux's -i at 80-136 ms is already close to tgrep. The gap comes from the ASCII-lowercase trigrams tgrep folds into its postings at index time.

**Don't copy**
- The serial verification loop.
- The rooted per-component handle and GetFinalPathName containment checks. They are a security feature against symlink and reparse escapes; replace them with one open, plus a reparse-attribute check from the walk if needed.
- JSON filestamps (2.7 MB).
- Reading and hashing the whole files.bin at start-up.
- Parsing meta.json twice.
- The server sends every match row as one JSON line over TCP.
- The server reads cache misses serially (serve.rs:2161).
- No custom allocator is used, so there is nothing to copy there either.

**Freshness, stated plainly**
- One-shot: it never reads filestamps.json and never stats the tree. It takes candidates from the stale index but reads their contents live.
  - New files are missed.
  - A file whose edit adds the pattern is missed if its old content lacked the trigrams.
  - Edited files that still have the trigrams show the new lines.
  - Deleted files print a warning.
- Server: it detects staleness only at start-up. It writes serve.json first, then runs a background walk comparing {mtime seconds, size, plus ns modified and created timestamps} against filestamps.json. After that it relies on the notify watcher (ReadDirectoryChangesW, recursive, bursts coalesced over 25-100 ms) plus an hourly reconcile.
  - handle_search takes no snapshot_gate and does no watcher drain. The server therefore answers stale results during the start-up check and during the event-burst window. It is NOT read-your-writes, so a loomux daemon copying this design needs an explicit barrier.

**Measurement caveats**
My walls (Search 100 ms / Search|Grep 123 ms / -i Search 202 ms / [A-Z]{3}\w+ 5955 ms, warm, Git Bash, stdout to /dev/null) are higher than the brief's 25/70/95-120/5200 ms. --stats and how I timed it differ. In-process times inside search_local_index were 43 / 57 / 145 / 5894 ms.

Careful: `tgrep -i search .` parses `search` as the subcommand, with '.' as the pattern, which yields MatchAll and 15 M matches. Check that the brief's -i benchmark did not fall into this.

**Benchmark path**
The default index directory is .tgrep (builder.rs:20), so the benchmark must have used `--index-path .cache/tgrep-index`. That path skips the shared-daemon .git probe (protocol.rs:73).

**Best levers for loomux (ranked)**
1. Prescan the whole buffer and keep a lazy line table instead of matching per line (COPY 2).
2. Read in one pass, fuse NUL detection into it, and skip mmap for small files (COPY 3).
3. Fold ASCII-lowercase trigrams into the postings for -i (COPY 1).
4. Keep the lookup table in a lazy mmap with binary search, so start-up does no table load (COPY 4).
5. Use the index only for files with an unchanged stamp and fully scan changed or new ones. This is the only design here that stays correct without a daemon (COPY 5).
6. For the daemon direction: an overlay plus a decoded-content LRU plus parallel matching, with a freshness barrier that tgrep lacks (COPY 6).

rt.notes:
Summary for the question of what loomux can take from tgrep:
(1) tgrep one-shot is fast only because it trusts the index blindly: no walk, no stat. Cost is about 9.5 ms process start + about 8 ms index open + 0.24-0.87 ms per candidate file read. On a modified tree it is wrong: the index here was already stale on 2 files, and new files are invisible even when a -g glob names them. loomux cannot take this over without dropping its correctness requirement.
(2) Every tree walk in tgrep is slower than loomux's 27 ms: count-files 78 ms, serve stale check 103 ms, --no-index 480-650 ms.
(3) tgrep's indexed verification path looks serial and is about 10x slower per file than its own brute-force path (6681 ms vs 648 ms for the no-literal regex). -j has no effect. loomux already beats it there.
(4) The real speed lever is the server: a resident index plus a file content cache plus a native watcher. Warm queries take 0.2-3 ms on the server side and about 17-25 ms at the client, and the floor there is client process start. Cold queries pay the same file-read cost as one-shot. The server is eventually consistent (an edit becomes visible after about 40-65 ms, and a query right after a write misses). If loomux wants this, it needs a resident daemon with a content cache and watcher, plus a read-your-writes barrier (for example a cheap stat of dirty paths, or waiting for the watcher queue to drain) to keep its correctness requirement.
(5) The index format is simple: a 16-byte fixed lookup record (trigram, u64 offset, u32 count) and uncompressed 6-byte postings. The index opens in 8 ms for 22 MB.

Housekeeping: the server ran on a copy of the index (scratchpad\idxcopy), because serve rewrites its index directory (the copy afterwards had changed sizes, a .retired directory and serve.json). md5sum -c confirms the original .cache/tgrep-index is unchanged (all OK). The server was stopped via Stop-Process. The exit code 127 of the background task comes from that kill. `tgrep status` reports `Server: not running`, and no tgrep.exe process remains. zz_tgrep_probe.go is deleted (`ls: cannot access`).

3. The trace marks are coarse. 'loadGraph' starts at init of the query package, not at Grep entry. With --no-refresh it shows 1.0 ms, so in the plugin call it is effectively freshness.Probe: walk + fingerprint gob + compare. I took the walk-only figure (27-35 ms) from the doc. No mark sits between the walk and the fingerprint read, and none inside 'trigram' (13 MB read vs Digest vs lookup) or 'search' (reads vs regex vs JSON spans vs Enclosing).

4. Discrepancy: the alternation 'search' phase measured 27-44 ms, against the doc's 9-12 ms after LITPRE. GODEBUG=gctrace=1 shows GC at about 3% and only one concurrent cycle in that phase, so GC does not explain it. The gap remains unexplained; the likely candidates are the case-folded prefilter passing 488 files, the asciiLower copies, and the per-file JSON unmarshal of spans.

5. The binary contains the spike symbols (spikeWhole, spikeLazySpans, lazyPostings). zz_spike_parwalk.go (23:55) is newer than spike.exe (23:35); SpikeResetWalk is not in the binary, so only that helper differs from what ran.

The parts loomux could still cut without dropping correctness are mostly the about 20 ms of whole-file state reads and recomputation (phases 4-9 minus the lookup) and about 5 ms of unneeded inits and image load. The walk (about 30-40 ms with the fingerprint compare) and the about 13-15 ms process start remain the floor.
